name: Alloy-Waste
geological_features: Metallic desert pavement of naturally alloyed minerals
Towering sandstone formations shaped by millennia of wind
Dead ocean basins now filled with mineral sand
specific_features: Colony settlement in the most temperate zone
Temporal distortion zone in the deepest basin
description: Alloy-Waste is a large desert world whose surface is paved with naturally occurring metallic alloys, wind-polished plates of mixed iron, copper, and nickel that tile the ground like the scales of an enormous reptile. Between these metallic pavements, sandy basins that were once ocean floors support hardy desert flora that has adapted to extract moisture from the metal-rich substrate. Towering sandstone formations, sculpted by persistent winds into flowing organic shapes, provide the only vertical relief on an otherwise flat and gleaming landscape.

The metallic ground creates unique acoustic properties, reflecting sound rather than absorbing it, so that footsteps ring out clearly and voices carry over improbable distances. The breathable atmosphere supports a hot, dry climate with extreme diurnal temperature swings, and the cooling metal plates produce a chorus of ticking and pinging at sunset that builds to a crescendo before subsiding into the cold silence of night. Desert flora blooms in brief, explosive displays after rare rain events, turning the metallic landscape temporarily lush with vegetation.

A colony has been established in the most temperate zone, its population drawn by the metallic resources literally underfoot and the solar potential of cloudless skies. The deepest former ocean basin harbors a temporal distortion zone where instruments record time passing at subtly different rates, an anomaly that has been stable for as long as measurements have been taken. The basin's metallic pavement shows wear patterns that suggest it was once the site of heavy traffic, though by what or whom remains unknown.

The colony is thriving, its economy built on the harvest of naturally alloyed metal plates that require minimal processing for industrial use. The temporal distortion zone has attracted research interest, though the anomaly's subtlety makes it difficult to study; the time differential amounts to mere seconds per hour, enough to desynchronize electronics but not dramatic enough for definitive conclusions about its nature. The desert flora's ability to extract metal compounds from the substrate is being studied for potential terraforming applications on other mineral-rich worlds.
